findings.issue_text: [BUG] The code depends on queue.Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown, which only exist in Python 3.13+. On any Python version below 3.13, FixedQueuePool.shutdown() crashes with AttributeError: 'Queue' object has no attribute 'shutdown', and every `except queue.ShutDown` clause raises AttributeError when evaluated, so the graceful-shutdown path the PR advertises never works — workers hang in work_queue.get() and daemon threads are killed mid-processing on interpreter exit.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() shut down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool, but ResultsStrategyFactory reuses the same queue_pool instance for every create_with_partitions call, so after any close arroyo creates a new strategy whose workers are all dead. On a partition rebalance (arroyo closes the old strategy then asks the factory for a new one), the new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy submits WorkItems to queues whose OrderedQueueWorker threads have exited; messages accumulate forever, result processing silently stops, and offsets are never committed for those partitions.

[BUG] get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(group_key), which is salted per-process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so group→queue assignment is not stable across restarts or sibling consumer processes. Two processes consuming the same topic (the CLI supports --processes > 1 with num_processes, which forks children) hash the same subscription key to different queue indices, so ordering guarantees for a subscription are broken by process boundaries; tests like test_different_groups_distributed (asserting len(queue_indices) == 3 over 20 keys) also become seed-dependent and can fail intermittently in CI.

[ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run wraps every single message in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(op="queue_worker.process", ...), creating a full SDK transaction per Kafka message on the hot consume path. At uptime-results volume this multiplies SDK overhead and transaction-span allocation per message across 20+ worker threads, degrading throughput and flooding any tracing backend wired up; a plain span (or nothing) would carry the same information.

[ADVISORY] The strategy feeds message.payload directly to decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload), which begins with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, so a FilteredPayload reaches the generic except branch and is logged as an unexpected error rather than being filtered cleanly. Any arroyo filter step upstream of this strategy turns filtered messages into a logged exception storm with full stack traces per message, and the offset is silently marked complete — operators see 'Error submitting message to queue' errors in logs while processing is actually fine, masking real errors.

[ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker never calls work_queue.task_done(), and FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty/Close rely on qsize() polling, which is a race-prone signal for completion. Any caller relying on wait_until_empty or get_stats to conclude processing finished (as the new tests do) can observe total_items == 0 while a worker is still mid-processing of the last dequeued item, so a shutdown or test assertion observes work as complete before the result_processor has actually returned.

[ADVISORY] ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() sets self.queue_pool = None while a live SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's commit loop and workers still reference the pool through the strategy, and create_with_partitions asserts self.queue_pool is not None. If shutdown races with a rebalance-triggered create_with_partitions (or the commit loop iterates after shutdown), the assert fails or the pool is used after its workers are joined; the generic try/except in the commit loop hides it as logged exceptions, so operators see silent commit stoppages during deploys.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks the class-level __call__ of the result processor with side_effect = [Exception("Processing failed"), None] but makes no assertion tying which message failed, and the final assert accepts len(committed_offsets) == 0 — the test passes even if no commit mechanism runs at all. The test named 'error_handling' cannot fail on the behavior it claims to validate (that a failed message does not block other commits while still being skipped in the contiguous run), so a regression that never commits after errors would ship undetected.

[ADVISORY] The Kafka integration test monkey-patches factory.create_with_partitions with an instance attribute assignment and drives processor._run_once()/processor._shutdown() via private arroyo APIs, coupling the test to arroyo internals that are not part of any stable contract. The next arroyo upgrade that renames _run_once or changes StreamProcessor internals breaks this test at CI time for everyone, and the method-assignment patch also silently bypasses any factory bookkeeping added to create_with_partitions later.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run's finally block unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset even when result_processor raised, so failed messages are marked complete and their offsets are committed to Kafka, permanently dropping the uptime result. A transient DB/processor error for a check result silently discards that result forever (offset committed, no retry, no dead-letter); additionally the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts `test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which the code contradicts — both messages are completed, the commit loop commits offset 102 within its 1s tick, so the assertion only passes by timing luck and will flake/fail deterministically once the commit fires.

[ADVISORY] close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before draining the queue pool, so items processed after the final commit-loop pass are never committed. On every graceful shutdown, the last batch of processed results is redelivered after restart (at-least-once with reprocessing side effects), and no test verifies that pending items submitted before shutdown are actually processed — test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown calls factory.shutdown() immediately after submit and only asserts `factory.queue_pool is None`, never asserting the 5 results were processed, so the 'no item is lost' guarantee the class docstring claims has zero verification.

[ADVISORY] Any exception raised inside the finally block (e.g. metrics.gauge failing) kills the worker thread's run() loop with no restart or watchdog, and the worker has no failure-signal surface. One dead worker permanently stops its queue: every group hashed to that queue stops being processed, its offsets stay outstanding forever, get_committable_offsets returns nothing for that partition, and the entire consumer stalls committing (head-of-line blocking) until the process is restarted — nothing in the diff detects or reports this state.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is dead code with zero call sites in the diff, and WorkItem.message is written on every submit but never read by any worker or commit path. Deleting wait_until_empty and the message field removes ~15 lines and the misleading implication that shutdown waits for drain (it does not — shutdown uses queue.shutdown instead), reducing the chance the next maintainer calls the wrong drain primitive during a shutdown refactor.

[ADVISORY] The click help text for --mode still reads 'Parallel uses multithreading' and does not document thread-queue-parallel's ordering guarantee or that max_workers controls queue count in that mode, while the sibling option --max-workers help was updated. An operator selecting thread-queue-parallel via the CLI has no indication that max_workers becomes the number of ordered queues (defaulting to 20, unrelated to thread count elsewhere), so they will misconfigure parallelism; the updated sibling-flag text without updating this one is exactly the sibling-propagation miss on the same option group.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run's `finally` block unconditionally calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised, so failed messages are marked processed and committed, directly violating the strategy's stated guarantee "No item is lost ... Only commits offsets after successful processing". Any exception in result_processor causes that uptime result to be silently dropped and its offset committed to Kafka, so the check result is permanently lost with no retry and no blocking of the commit; the diff's own error-handling test (test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling) asserts this lossy behavior rather than the documented guarantee.

[ADVISORY] WorkItem.message ("includes the original message for offset tracking") is populated at submit time but never read anywhere in the diff — offset tracking uses only partition/offset. The next maintainer must copy a full arroyo Message (payload bytes included) into every work item for no consumer; deleting the field removes a per-item memory pin (the whole Kafka payload stays referenced while queued) and one constructor argument at every call site.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is dead code — no caller in the diff or in the factory wiring uses it, and its correctness is dubious anyway (qsize()==0 does not mean items finished processing since workers may hold an item outside the queue). Any future caller relying on it for graceful-drain logic gets a false 'empty' signal while a worker still holds an in-flight item whose offset is not yet complete; deleting it removes the misleading API and 9 lines.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds unconditional module-level imports of confluent_kafka Producer/Consumer/AdminClient, arroyo KafkaConsumer/StreamProcessor, and django settings-derived kafka helpers to a test file whose existing (non-Kafka) tests never need them; only the new requires_kafka-marked class uses them. Every run of the large existing ProcessResultTest suite now pays kafka client import/setup cost and breaks entirely in environments without a kafka-capable confluent_kafka install, despite the requires_kafka marker existing precisely to gate this.

[ADVISORY] test_different_groups_distributed asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` for 20 hash-assigned groups, which is not guaranteed by consistent hashing — two of the three queues can legitimately receive zero of those 20 groups under some PYTHONHASHSEED values. The test intermittently fails (and will look like a product bug) purely due to per-process string-hash randomization; asserting coverage of all queues by a keyed distribution is an invariant the implementation does not promise.

[BUG] The worker's `finally` block calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset` unconditionally, so a message whose `result_processor` raised is still marked completed and its offset gets committed by the commit loop. When a result fails to process (DB error, bad payload downstream of the decoder), the offset is committed anyway, so on consumer restart that message is never redelivered — the uptime check result is permanently lost, contradicting the class docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. The at-least-once contract is silently converted to at-most-once.

[BUG] Each pool queue is created as an unbounded `queue.Queue()`, so the strategy's submit() never blocks and there is no backpressure despite the docstring claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. If the worker threads fall behind (slow result_processor, DB contention), arroyo's poll thread keeps enqueuing messages into unbounded in-memory queues; the consumer balloons in memory and offsets lag indefinitely on a hot path with no bound, and no metric or signal tells the operator to intervene.

[BUG] `get_committable_offsets` iterates `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without holding any lock while `add_offset` (called from arroyo's poll thread via submit) can insert a new partition into the defaultdict concurrently, raising 'dictionary changed size during iteration'. When a rebalance assigns a new partition and its first message arrives while the 1-second commit loop is snapshotting the key list, the commit thread's `list()` raises RuntimeError; the exception is swallowed by the loop's broad except, but a crash at that moment also skips mark_committed, and repeated collisions can stall commits and leak all_offsets entries until the next successful iteration.

[ADVISORY] The FixedQueuePool and its OffsetTracker are constructed once on the factory and shared across every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy instance created by `create_with_partitions`, while each strategy instance spawns its own commit thread bound to that call's `commit` callable. On a Kafka rebalance, the old strategy's commit thread can still be alive briefly, committing offsets for partitions that were revoked (via the stale commit callable) and interleaving mark_committed with the new strategy's tracker state; operators see committed-offset confusion or double commits during every rebalance in thread-queue-parallel mode.

[ADVISORY] `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate()` calls `queue_pool.shutdown()` which uses `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, draining the full in-flight backlog instead of aborting. When arroyo invokes terminate() (e.g., a hard error or forced shutdown), the intent is immediate abort, but the pool drains every queued uptime result before the 5-second join timeout — a stuck result_processor makes terminate hang for the full timeout per shutdown path, delaying consumer group rebalance for other members.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling encodes the contract 'a failed message blocks offset commits' but only passes because it checks committed_offsets ~0.2s after the queues drain, while the commit loop runs on a 1-second tick — so the test goes green while the code (per the finally-block finding) commits the failed message's offset shortly after. The suite certifies that failed results are not committed while production commits and drops them; any engineer relying on this test to reason about failure semantics in thread-queue-parallel mode gets the opposite of real behavior, and the test will flip to red nondeterminically on a slow CI box.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run's finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset unconditionally, so offsets for messages whose result_processor raised are marked complete and committed even though processing failed. The class docstrings in this diff promise 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but a failed handle_result (e.g. a DB error while updating an uptime monitor) is logged and its offset is committed anyway, permanently skipping the uptime result — silent data loss that the previous serial/parallel consumers would have surfaced as a redelivery or crash.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's generic except handler marks the message's offset as add+complete, so any decoder or grouping_fn failure causes the message to be treated as successfully processed and its offset committed. A poison message (schema change, decode error) is logged once and then committed, so it is never redelivered and the uptime check result is silently dropped; the exception path's own intent (quarantine/redelivery) is inverted into a commit path.

[BUG] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no commit occurs after a processing failure, which contradicts the implementation in queue_consumer.py that completes (and thus commits) the failed offset in the worker's finally block; the test only passes by timing luck because it returns after a 0.2s sleep before the 1s commit loop ticks. The test suite enshrines the intended behavior (failures block commits) while the code implements the opposite, so the intent violation ships masked by a flaky test that flips to failure on any timing change, and CI provides no protection against the data-loss commit behavior.

[ADVISORY] The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but the pool uses unbounded queue.Queue instances, so there is no backpressure of any kind. An operator tuning the new thread-queue-parallel mode based on the documented guarantee gets unbounded memory growth and rising queue_depth gauges during result-processor slowdowns instead of the promised producer-side slowdown; the docstring is the only spec of the mode's intent and it is false.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group uses Python's builtin hash(), which for str is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the group→queue assignment documented as 'consistent hashing' changes on every process restart. The 'No dynamic reassignment that could break ordering' guarantee holds only within a single process lifetime; after a restart mid-backlog, in-flight uncommitted messages for the same subscription can be processed by a different queue while older redelivered messages land on another, so consumers of the ordered-processing guarantee (uptime incident state transitions) see ordering violations across restarts even though no code path in this diff changes assignment dynamically.

[ADVISORY] terminate() shuts down the pool but never joins the commit thread, and the subsequent arroyo join() calls close(), which restarts shutdown_event-set and calls queue_pool.shutdown() a second time, double-invoking worker joins and queue.shutdown on already-shut-down queues. On the arroyo terminate path (broker error, rebalance), the commit thread can still be mid-commit_function when the strategy is torn down, and the double-shutdown path exercises q.shutdown() on shut-down queues, converting what the parent consumer treats as a controlled termination into logged 'Error shutting down queue' noise and possible commit-after-close calls to a revoked consumer.

[BUG] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's final assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` is a tautology that passes whether or not commits occur, so the test verifies nothing about error handling. The `or` makes the test pass in both worlds: it cannot detect that OrderedQueueWorker.run's `finally: self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` (queue_consumer.py) marks failed messages complete, so the offsets of messages whose result_processor raised ARE committed — failed uptime results are silently dropped and never retried, and this data-loss behavior ships unflagged because the test green-lights it.

[BUG] Every thread-queue-parallel mode test patches `type(factory.result_processor).__call__`, replacing the unit under test with a mock, so the real result-processing logic is never exercised in the new mode. mock_processor_call.assert_has_calls([call("uptime", result_1), ...]) verifies only that the mock was invoked with the decoded payloads; a regression in how the strategy decodes, groups, or hands results to the real UptimeResultProcessor exclusively in thread-queue-parallel mode (e.g. decode_payload's `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` raising inside the new strategy's submit) passes all these tests, since the same mocking pattern recurs in test_thread_queue_parallel, _preserves_order, _concurrent_subscriptions, _offset_commit, _error_handling, _offset_gaps, and the Kafka integration test.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown asserts only `factory.queue_pool is None` after shutdown and never asserts the 5 submitted messages were processed, so the 'graceful' claim in its name is unverified. If the shutdown path (queue.shutdown(immediate=False) after setting worker.shutdown=True, plus the worker break on queue.ShutDown) drops all in-flight items, the test still passes — the next engineer touching FixedQueuePool.shutdown gets no signal that queued work must drain.

[ADVISORY] test_concurrent_processing_across_groups asserts only that all 6 items completed and that 3 distinct groups were seen — nothing asserts actual concurrency (no overlap timing, no parallel execution check), so the test passes with a fully serial implementation. A regression that collapses FixedQueuePool to a single worker (breaking the PR's entire purpose) passes this test and test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, which has the same shape; the headline property of the diff — parallelism — is asserted nowhere.

[ADVISORY] test_stats_reporting's `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` is a race: the 3 already-started worker threads can fully drain the 10 queued items before get_stats() runs, making the assertion flaky, and it verifies only non-emptiness, not stats correctness. The test intermittently fails on slow/loaded CI purely due to worker scheduling speed, and when it passes it has not checked that queue_depths/total_items actually reflect queue contents for any invariant beyond `> 0`.

[ADVISORY] test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy asserts only types and configuration (isinstance, num_queues==5) and never submits a message through the created strategy, so the factory-to-strategy wiring (commit_offsets +1 translation, decode_payload partial, grouping_fn) in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker is untested at this layer. A bug in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker such as swapping the +1 offset translation or passing the wrong grouping function is only catchable by the uptime-specific tests; the generic remote_subscriptions factory path has no end-to-end test, and other consumers adopting the mode inherit unverified wiring.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run() swallows exceptions from result_processor and still marks the offset complete in the finally block, so the commit loop will commit past the failed message and Kafka will never redeliver it. A transient DB error or any exception while handling an uptime result (e.g. a deadlocked update on ProjectUptimeSubscription) is logged and discarded; the offset is committed within 1 second and the check result is permanently lost, whereas the serial/parallel modes crash the consumer and force redelivery. This is silent data loss of monitor results.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s broad except handler marks any message that raised during decode/submit as completed, which makes a poison payload (or a persistent decode bug) silently consumed and its offset committed rather than surfacing the failure. If decode_payload raises systematically (schema/codec mismatch after a producer deploy), every affected message is logged once per message, marked complete, and committed; the entire topic is silently drained with zero results processed and no consumer failure to alert on. Note in the real factory decode_payload asserts `not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, so every filtered message also goes through this exception path.

[ADVISORY] The per-group work queues are unbounded queue.Queue instances with no maxsize, so despite the class docstring's claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the strategy imposes no backpressure at all. If processing falls behind (slow result_processor, e.g. a DB outage where every call takes seconds), the arroyo consumer keeps polling and enqueueing without bound; a single consumer process accumulates unbounded in-memory WorkItems (each holding the full Kafka message) until OOM kills the worker, which also loses every queued, uncommitted message.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before q.shutdown(immediate=False), but a worker already blocked inside result_processor (or one that grabs an item between the shutdown-flag check and queue shutdown) will finish that item and complete its offset after SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() has already joined the commit thread, so that final completed offset is never committed. On every graceful restart the last in-flight message per partition is reprocessed after rebalance; for non-idempotent result handling this means duplicate processing of uptime results on every deploy. Additionally terminate() (arroyo's error path) skips committing completed work entirely and abandons queued items, so a crash-looping consumer redelivers a full queue's worth of messages each cycle.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the Kafka offset in the finally block even when result_processor raised, so failed messages are permanently lost while their offsets are committed. Any exception in result_processor (DB error, decode downstream, transient network failure) is logged and then the offset is marked complete; the commit loop commits past the failed message and Kafka never redelivers it, so the uptime result is silently dropped with no retry — exactly the silent-partial-success the class docstring claims cannot happen ("Only commits offsets after successful processing" is false).

[BUG] FixedQueuePool.shutdown never actually stops workers blocked in work_queue.get(), because the per-worker shutdown flag is only checked at the top of the loop and Queue.shutdown semantics are mishandled. Workers sit blocked in get() with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown = True` flag is unobservable until a new item arrives; q.shutdown(immediate=False) raises (unfinished tasks, since task_done is never called) or, on Python < 3.13, queue.Queue has no shutdown method at all — the AttributeError is swallowed by `except Exception` in shutdown, so every worker.join(timeout=5.0) times out, threads leak per factory construction, and any queued items are dropped without their offsets being committed.

[ADVISORY] get_committable_offsets iterates the full `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every 1-second commit tick, and all_offsets grows without bound while any hole persists. On a partition with a long-lived processing gap (a slow group, a hung DB call for one subscription), the commit thread burns O(offset-span) CPU each second — with a 10M-offset spread that is millions of iterations per tick per partition — and the all_offsets set for that partition keeps growing; operators see the consumer peg a core and memory creep with no signal other than the commit metric going quiet.

[ADVISORY] The FixedQueuePool and its OffsetTracker are created once on the factory and shared across every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions, so on a partition rebalance the old strategy's commit thread keeps running and keeps committing offsets for partitions it no longer owns using a stale Commit callback. During a consumer-group rebalance, the previous strategy's _commit_loop (its shutdown_event was never set — only factory.shutdown stops it, and create_with_partitions doesn't close the old strategy) commits offsets for revoked partitions through the invalidated commit, racing the new owner and producing premature commits on another consumer's behalf; repeated rebalances also stack up one leaked commit thread per strategy.

[ADVISORY] wait_until_empty reports success based solely on qsize()==0, counting items already dequeued but still being processed as done. A caller polling emptiness to decide safe shutdown (the natural use, since close() does not drain) sees "empty" while a worker is mid-flight on the last item and proceeds, so shutdown drops that item; currently no in-diff caller uses it, but it is exported API that invites exactly the drop-on-shutdown bug it purports to guard.

[ADVISORY] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which blocks up to num_queues × 5s serially in worker joins. Arroyo invokes join(timeout) expecting a bounded wait; with 20 queues the shutdown can block for over 100 seconds (each hung worker consumes its own full 5s join), so consumer shutdown/rebalance timeouts fire and the process is SIGKILLed, losing all in-flight offsets for partitions it still owns.

[ADVISORY] get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash(), which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so group→queue assignment differs across restarts and across worker processes in the same deployment. Two processes consuming the same subscription groups assign them to different internal queues; within a single process restart, any group being processed when the process dies resumes on a different worker with no ordering guarantee relative to messages handled earlier — the "consistent hashing" the class docstring promises does not survive a restart, silently relaxing the ordering guarantee during deploys.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` the diff introduces `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` while the docstring claims “consistent hashing” and “No dynamic reassignment that could break ordering.” Python’s built-in `hash(str)` is salted per process by default, so the group→queue mapping is not stable across restarts. That’s a real, diff-grounded concern/mismatch between the documented guarantee and actual behavior, but the finding’s specific claim about ordering violations “across restarts mid-backlog” is not directly verifiable from the diff (after a restart there are no in-flight work items; ordering within a run is still preserved per-group).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] terminate() shuts down the pool but never joins the commit thread, and the subsequent arroyo join() calls close(), which restarts shutdown_event-set and calls queue_pool.shutdown() a second time, double-invoking worker joins and queue.shutdown on already-shut-down queues. On the arroyo terminate path (broker error, rebalance), the commit thread can still be mid-commit_function when the strategy is torn down, and the double-shutdown path exercises q.shutdown() on shut-down queues, converting what the parent consumer treats as a controlled termination into logged 'Error shutting down queue' noise and possible commit-after-close calls to a revoked consumer.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (new file `queue_consumer.py`), `terminate()` only does `self.shutdown_event.set()` and `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` but never joins `self.commit_thread` (unlike `close()`, which does `self.commit_thread.join(...)`). Also, `join()` unconditionally calls `self.close()`. If Arroyo calls `terminate()` and then `join()` (a common lifecycle), `queue_pool.shutdown()` will be invoked twice (`terminate()` then `close()`), and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` will re-run `q.shutdown(...)` and worker joins, potentially triggering the logged `"Error shutting down queue"` path. Additionally, without joining the commit thread on `terminate()`, the commit loop can still be mid-`commit_function(...)` while teardown proceeds, which matches the finding’s concern about commit-after-terminate behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling's final assertion `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` is a tautology that passes whether or not commits occur, so the test verifies nothing about error handling. The `or` makes the test pass in both worlds: it cannot detect that OrderedQueueWorker.run's `finally: self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` (queue_consumer.py) marks failed messages complete, so the offsets of messages whose result_processor raised ARE committed — failed uptime results are silently dropped and never retried, and this data-loss behavior ships unflagged because the test green-lights it.

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so offsets are marked complete even when `result_processor` raises. The commit loop (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`) then sees those offsets as committable and will call `commit_function`, meaning failed messages can still be committed (and thus dropped/no retry) — a real data-loss/correctness issue that contradicts the strategy docstring (“Only commits offsets after successful processing”). The finding’s claim that the test assertion is a tautology is inaccurate (it would fail if `test_partition` were committed), but the underlying behavior it points to is a real defect introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Every thread-queue-parallel mode test patches `type(factory.result_processor).__call__`, replacing the unit under test with a mock, so the real result-processing logic is never exercised in the new mode. mock_processor_call.assert_has_calls([call("uptime", result_1), ...]) verifies only that the mock was invoked with the decoded payloads; a regression in how the strategy decodes, groups, or hands results to the real UptimeResultProcessor exclusively in thread-queue-parallel mode (e.g. decode_payload's `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` raising inside the new strategy's submit) passes all these tests, since the same mocking pattern recurs in test_thread_queue_parallel, _preserves_order, _concurrent_subscriptions, _offset_commit, _error_handling, _offset_gaps, and the Kafka integration test.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added uptime tests for `mode="thread-queue-parallel"` (e.g. `test_thread_queue_parallel`, `_preserves_order`, `_concurrent_subscriptions`, `_offset_commit`, `_error_handling`, `_offset_gaps`, and the Kafka integration test), the code repeatedly patches `type(factory.result_processor).__call__` (e.g. `with mock.patch.object(type(factory.result_processor), "__call__") as mock_processor_call:`), which prevents exercising the real `UptimeResultProcessor` logic in this new mode. However, this does not replace/skip the strategy’s decode/group/queue plumbing: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` still runs `decoder(...)` and `grouping_fn(...)` before invoking the (mocked) processor, so failures like `decode_payload` raising would typically reduce call counts and fail these assertions. The review point is therefore mainly about test coverage depth for real processor behavior under the new mode, not a demonstrable functional defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown asserts only `factory.queue_pool is None` after shutdown and never asserts the 5 submitted messages were processed, so the 'graceful' claim in its name is unverified. If the shutdown path (queue.shutdown(immediate=False) after setting worker.shutdown=True, plus the worker break on queue.ShutDown) drops all in-flight items, the test still passes — the next engineer touching FixedQueuePool.shutdown gets no signal that queued work must drain.

adjudication.rationale: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` (added in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py`), the test enqueues 5 results via `self.send_result(...)` and then immediately calls `factory.shutdown()` and asserts only `factory.queue_pool is None`. It never asserts that the 5 submitted messages were actually processed (e.g., via the patched processor call count or queue drain), so the test name’s “graceful shutdown” behavior (draining queued work before stopping) is not verified by this test. The finding’s specific concern about shutdown potentially dropping work is plausible, but the key point—test does not validate draining—is directly grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_concurrent_processing_across_groups asserts only that all 6 items completed and that 3 distinct groups were seen — nothing asserts actual concurrency (no overlap timing, no parallel execution check), so the test passes with a fully serial implementation. A regression that collapses FixedQueuePool to a single worker (breaking the PR's entire purpose) passes this test and test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions, which has the same shape; the headline property of the diff — parallelism — is asserted nowhere.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py`, `test_concurrent_processing_across_groups` only waits for completion (`process_complete_event`) and then asserts `len(self.processed_items) == 6` and that 3 group IDs were observed; it never measures overlap/timing or verifies that more than one worker is active, so a fully serial implementation (or a regression to a single worker) could still pass. Similarly, in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions` only asserts `mock_processor_call.call_count == 2` after the queues drain; it does not assert parallel execution. This is a diff-grounded gap in testing the new mode's headline property (parallelism), not a direct functional bug in the implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_stats_reporting's `assert stats["total_items"] > 0` is a race: the 3 already-started worker threads can fully drain the 10 queued items before get_stats() runs, making the assertion flaky, and it verifies only non-emptiness, not stats correctness. The test intermittently fails on slow/loaded CI purely due to worker scheduling speed, and when it passes it has not checked that queue_depths/total_items actually reflect queue contents for any invariant beyond `> 0`.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting`, the `FixedQueuePool` starts worker threads immediately in `setUp()` (workers are `daemon=True` and started in `FixedQueuePool.__init__`). The test enqueues 10 items via `self.pool.submit(...)` and then immediately calls `stats = self.pool.get_stats()` and asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. Because workers may drain the queues very quickly (no blocking/synchronization before `get_stats()`), `total_items` can legitimately be 0 at that point, making this assertion timing-dependent/flaky. The finding’s second point is also accurate: the test only checks non-emptiness, not that `queue_depths`/`total_items` reflect a specific expected invariant at a well-defined moment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy asserts only types and configuration (isinstance, num_queues==5) and never submits a message through the created strategy, so the factory-to-strategy wiring (commit_offsets +1 translation, decode_payload partial, grouping_fn) in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker is untested at this layer. A bug in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker such as swapping the +1 offset translation or passing the wrong grouping function is only catchable by the uptime-specific tests; the generic remote_subscriptions factory path has no end-to-end test, and other consumers adopting the mode inherit unverified wiring.

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py`, `TestThreadQueueParallelIntegration.test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy` only checks that the factory returns a `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and that `factory.queue_pool.num_queues == 5`. It does not submit any `Message` through the created strategy, so it does not exercise the wiring inside `ResultsStrategyFactory.create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, including the `commit_offsets` +1 translation (`commit_data = {partition: offset + 1 ...}`), the `decoder=partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)`, or that `grouping_fn=self.build_payload_grouping_key` is actually used. Other tests cover `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`/`FixedQueuePool` behavior directly and uptime has deeper integration tests, but the generic factory-to-strategy glue for remote_subscriptions is not validated end-to-end here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run() swallows exceptions from result_processor and still marks the offset complete in the finally block, so the commit loop will commit past the failed message and Kafka will never redeliver it. A transient DB error or any exception while handling an uptime result (e.g. a deadlocked update on ProjectUptimeSubscription) is logged and discarded; the offset is committed within 1 second and the check result is permanently lost, whereas the serial/parallel modes crash the consumer and force redelivery. This is silent data loss of monitor results.

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception from `self.result_processor(self.identifier, work_item.result)` is caught by the broad `except Exception:` which only logs (`logger.exception(...)`) and then continues. Regardless of success/failure, the `finally` block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`. Since `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` commits any offsets deemed committable by `OffsetTracker` (and then `mark_committed`), a failed processing attempt will still be treated as completed and can be committed, preventing Kafka redelivery and causing silent data loss for that message.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()'s broad except handler marks any message that raised during decode/submit as completed, which makes a poison payload (or a persistent decode bug) silently consumed and its offset committed rather than surfacing the failure. If decode_payload raises systematically (schema/codec mismatch after a producer deploy), every affected message is logged once per message, marked complete, and committed; the entire topic is silently drained with zero results processed and no consumer failure to alert on. Note in the real factory decode_payload asserts `not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, so every filtered message also goes through this exception path.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception during `decoder(message.payload)` or subsequent logic is caught by a broad `except Exception`, logged, and then the code explicitly `add_offset`+`complete_offset` for that message (when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`). That makes the offset eligible for commit in `_commit_loop` even though processing failed, allowing systematic decode/codec failures (or poison payloads) to be silently skipped and committed. Additionally, since the real factory passes `partial(self.decode_payload, ...)` and `decode_payload` asserts `not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, a `FilteredPayload` would raise and go through this same “mark complete” path, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The per-group work queues are unbounded queue.Queue instances with no maxsize, so despite the class docstring's claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", the strategy imposes no backpressure at all. If processing falls behind (slow result_processor, e.g. a DB outage where every call takes seconds), the arroyo consumer keeps polling and enqueueing without bound; a single consumer process accumulates unbounded in-memory WorkItems (each holding the full Kafka message) until OOM kills the worker, which also loses every queued, uncommitted message.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each per-group queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (i.e., unbounded). In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, items are enqueued via `work_queue.put(work_item)` and there is no throttling/blocking mechanism elsewhere (poll only reports metrics). This directly contradicts the strategy docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and allows unbounded in-memory growth of `WorkItem`s (which include the full `Message`), making OOM and loss of uncommitted queued work a real failure mode when processing falls behind.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before q.shutdown(immediate=False), but a worker already blocked inside result_processor (or one that grabs an item between the shutdown-flag check and queue shutdown) will finish that item and complete its offset after SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() has already joined the commit thread, so that final completed offset is never committed. On every graceful restart the last in-flight message per partition is reprocessed after rebalance; for non-idempotent result handling this means duplicate processing of uptime results on every deploy. Additionally terminate() (arroyo's error path) skips committing completed work entirely and abandons queued items, so a crash-looping consumer redelivers a full queue's worth of messages each cycle.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, the shutdown event is set and the `commit_thread` is joined *before* shutting down the `queue_pool`/workers (`commit_thread.join(...); self.queue_pool.shutdown()`). Workers (`OrderedQueueWorker.run`) can still be processing an item (or finish one after `close()` stops the commit loop) and will call `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in `finally`, but there is no longer any commit loop running to observe those completed offsets and call `commit_function(...)`. This can leave the last in-flight offset(s) uncommitted on graceful shutdown, causing reprocessing after restart. The diff also shows `terminate()` similarly stops the commit loop (`shutdown_event.set()`) and immediately shuts down the pool without any final commit/drain step, so completed work near termination can be dropped from committing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the Kafka offset in the finally block even when result_processor raised, so failed messages are permanently lost while their offsets are committed. Any exception in result_processor (DB error, decode downstream, transient network failure) is logged and then the offset is marked complete; the commit loop commits past the failed message and Kafka never redelivers it, so the uptime result is silently dropped with no retry — exactly the silent-partial-success the class docstring claims cannot happen ("Only commits offsets after successful processing" is false).

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` is executed in the `finally` block unconditionally, even when `self.result_processor(...)` raises (it is caught by `except Exception:` and only logged). Since `FixedQueuePool.submit` always calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)`, a failed item will be removed from `outstanding` and thus becomes eligible in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`. The commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` will then call `commit_function` and `mark_committed`, allowing Kafka offsets to advance past failed messages with no retry path, contradicting the docstring claim "Only commits offsets after successful processing".

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] FixedQueuePool.shutdown never actually stops workers blocked in work_queue.get(), because the per-worker shutdown flag is only checked at the top of the loop and Queue.shutdown semantics are mishandled. Workers sit blocked in get() with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown = True` flag is unobservable until a new item arrives; q.shutdown(immediate=False) raises (unfinished tasks, since task_done is never called) or, on Python < 3.13, queue.Queue has no shutdown method at all — the AttributeError is swallowed by `except Exception` in shutdown, so every worker.join(timeout=5.0) times out, threads leak per factory construction, and any queued items are dropped without their offsets being committed.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, workers are signaled via `worker.shutdown = True`, but `OrderedQueueWorker.run` blocks indefinitely on `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the flag is not observed unless `get()` returns/raises. The shutdown path then tries `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, but `queue.Queue.shutdown`/`queue.ShutDown` are not guaranteed to exist (pre-Python 3.13), and any resulting exception (e.g., `AttributeError`) is swallowed, leaving threads blocked; `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` does not ensure termination. Additionally, items are enqueued via `put()` but the worker never calls `task_done()`, which makes any shutdown semantics that rely on unfinished-task tracking incorrect. This can lead to leaked threads and incomplete processing/commit progress on shutdown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] get_committable_offsets iterates the full `range(start, max_offset + 1)` for every partition on every 1-second commit tick, and all_offsets grows without bound while any hole persists. On a partition with a long-lived processing gap (a slow group, a hung DB call for one subscription), the commit thread burns O(offset-span) CPU each second — with a 10M-offset spread that is millions of iterations per tick per partition — and the all_offsets set for that partition keeps growing; operators see the consumer peg a core and memory creep with no signal other than the commit metric going quiet.

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` (new in `queue_consumer.py`), each 1s commit tick computes `min(all_offsets)` and `max(all_offsets)` for every partition and may iterate `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)`. Both `min`/`max` on a `set` are O(n) over `all_offsets`, and the `range` loop can be O(offset-span) until it hits the first missing/outstanding offset. Meanwhile `all_offsets[partition]` is only pruned in `mark_committed` (removes `<= offset`), so if progress can’t be committed past an early stuck/outstanding offset, newer offsets keep being `add_offset`’d and the set can grow very large, amplifying the per-tick work and memory usage. This is a concrete performance/resource-exhaustion defect in the added strategy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The FixedQueuePool and its OffsetTracker are created once on the factory and shared across every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by create_with_partitions, so on a partition rebalance the old strategy's commit thread keeps running and keeps committing offsets for partitions it no longer owns using a stale Commit callback. During a consumer-group rebalance, the previous strategy's _commit_loop (its shutdown_event was never set — only factory.shutdown stops it, and create_with_partitions doesn't close the old strategy) commits offsets for revoked partitions through the invalidated commit, racing the new owner and producing premature commits on another consumer's behalf; repeated rebalances also stack up one leaked commit thread per strategy.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ResultsStrategyFactory` constructs a single `FixedQueuePool` on the factory (`self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)` in `__init__`) and then reuses it for every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` returned by `create_with_partitions` (`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` passes `queue_pool=self.queue_pool`). Each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` instance starts its own background `commit_thread` in `__init__` (`self.commit_thread = threading.Thread(...); self.commit_thread.start()`) and will call the per-strategy `commit_function` passed from `create_with_partitions`. If multiple strategies are ever created from the same factory (e.g., during rebalances), this design can result in multiple commit threads operating concurrently against the same shared `OffsetTracker`/queue pool, potentially committing with a stale `commit` callback and/or leaking threads unless the old strategy is reliably closed/terminated. The diff itself doesn’t show any mechanism in `ResultsStrategyFactory.create_with_partitions` to retire prior strategies, and `factory.shutdown()` only shuts down the shared pool (not strategy threads), so the risk described is grounded in the added code structure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] wait_until_empty reports success based solely on qsize()==0, counting items already dequeued but still being processed as done. A caller polling emptiness to decide safe shutdown (the natural use, since close() does not drain) sees "empty" while a worker is mid-flight on the last item and proceeds, so shutdown drops that item; currently no in-diff caller uses it, but it is exported API that invites exactly the drop-on-shutdown bug it purports to guard.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty`, “emptiness” is computed as `sum(q.qsize() ...) == 0` via `get_stats()`, which indeed ignores work that has already been dequeued by a worker thread but is still executing in `OrderedQueueWorker.run`. So the method can return `True` while a worker is mid-flight on the last item. However, the finding’s stronger claim that this causes the item to be dropped on shutdown is not directly supported: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins workers (`worker.join(...)`), and a worker that is already processing will finish the current item before exiting its loop. The core issue is the misleading/insufficient “drained” signal, not a demonstrable drop-on-shutdown for the in-flight last item from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout argument and delegates to close(), which blocks up to num_queues × 5s serially in worker joins. Arroyo invokes join(timeout) expecting a bounded wait; with 20 queues the shutdown can block for over 100 seconds (each hung worker consumes its own full 5s join), so consumer shutdown/rebalance timeouts fire and the process is SIGKILLed, losing all in-flight offsets for partitions it still owns.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)`, the `timeout` parameter is ignored and the method unconditionally calls `self.close()` (new file `queue_consumer.py`). `close()` then calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker thread sequentially with `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` inside a loop over `self.workers`. With `num_queues` workers, worst-case shutdown wait is roughly `num_queues * 5s` (plus up to 5s for `commit_thread.join`), which is unbounded with respect to the `join(timeout)` argument. This is a concrete behavioral defect visible from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash(), which is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so group→queue assignment differs across restarts and across worker processes in the same deployment. Two processes consuming the same subscription groups assign them to different internal queues; within a single process restart, any group being processed when the process dies resumes on a different worker with no ordering guarantee relative to messages handled earlier — the "consistent hashing" the class docstring promises does not survive a restart, silently relaxing the ordering guarantee during deploys.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`, and Python’s built-in `hash()` is salt-randomized per process by default (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the “consistent hashing” claim in the docstring does not hold across process restarts or different processes. However, within a single process run, all items for a given `group_key` still deterministically map to the same queue/worker, so the core in-process ordering guarantee is preserved; the finding’s stronger claim about restart breaking ordering guarantees is largely speculative and not directly demonstrated by the diff.
